checks.location: Theorem1 Gaussian sketch proof and Theorem2 exponential sketch argument; Full AppendicesA–B, PDF pp.11–12
checks.claim: Theorem1 Gaussian sketch proof and Theorem2 exponential sketch argument; Full AppendicesA–B, PDF pp.11–12
checks.explanation: The relative inner-product estimate requires an exact zero after projection whenever the original inner product is zero. Gaussian projection does not preserve such zeros. The exponential-sketch argument has a separate failure: the proposed sketch produces a centered random output even on zero logits and constant values, whereas exact normalized attention returns one.
checks.demonstration: Set $Q=K=0$ and choose $w^\top=e_1-e_2$ as a column of $VW^V$. Then $$P=\frac{\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top}{n},\qquad Pw^\top=0,\qquad PR^\top Rw^\top=\frac{\mathbf1}{n}\bigl[\mathbf1^\top R^\top R(e_1-e_2)\bigr].$$ The bracketed quantity is a nonzero polynomial of continuously distributed Gaussian entries, so it vanishes with probability zero. The relative-error event is therefore impossible almost surely, even though its advertised lower bound is positive for sufficiently large $k$. For Appendix B, take $x=0$ and $y^\top=e_1-e_2$. With the proposed $F=e^{-\delta}R$, $$\exp(x)y^\top=0,\qquad\exp(xE^\top)Fy^\top=e^{-\delta}\mathbf1_k^\top R(e_1-e_2)\ne0\quad\text{almost surely}.$$ This directly contradicts the relative bound in Eq. (21). At the same input, the discrepancy in Eq. (23) is independent of $\delta$, so its appeal to local Lipschitz continuity cannot repair the construction. For the normalized bound itself, take $x=0$ and $v=\mathbf1_n$. Exact attention returns $1$, while the proposed construction returns $$Z=\frac{e^{-\delta}}{k}\mathbf1_k^\top R\mathbf1_n\sim N\!\left(0,\frac{e^{-2\delta}n}{k^2}\right).$$ Theorem 2 permits error $\varepsilon\|\mathbf1_n/n\|_2\|\mathbf1_n\|_2=\varepsilon$. For $0<\varepsilon<1$, its success interval $[1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon]$ is strictly positive, so the success probability is less than $1/2$. This cannot approach the claimed $1-o(1)$. Appendix B specifies $\delta=2^{-n}$ and later separately invokes $\delta=\theta(1/n)$; the zero-logit calculation holds for both choices.
checks.repair: For fixed attention matrix $P$ and value vector $v$, a valid Gaussian-projection argument gives $$\|(PR^\top R-P)v\|_2\leq\eta\|P\|_F\|v\|_2$$ with probability at least $1-4n\exp[-k(\eta^2/4-\eta^3/6)]$, for $0<\eta<1$. This follows by applying the squared-norm concentration bound to the sum and difference of normalized vector pairs, then taking a union bound over rows. To obtain relative output error, additionally require $\|Pv\|_2\geq\beta\|P\|_F\|v\|_2$ for some $\beta>0$ and choose $\eta=\varepsilon\beta$. The original assumptions provide no such margin. Finite input support permits a further union bound when inputs are fixed independently of the sketch. These changes repair only the first proof with a weaker guarantee. The second construction needs an approximation argument that controls exponential weights and the actual softmax denominator; shrinking $\delta$ does not supply it.
checks.scope: The counterexamples refute the supplied Gaussian constructions, including the normalized second construction. They are valid even when queries, keys and values arise from one token matrix, by choosing $W^Q=W^K=0$. For a single fixed nonzero value vector $v$, the rank-at-most-one matrix $\widetilde P=(Pv)v^\top/\|v\|_2^2$ reproduces the output exactly. Failure of the random construction therefore does not establish a low-rank impossibility, and alternative existential projections in Theorem 2 remain open here. Learned Linformer projections are outside these Gaussian-construction counterexamples.
checks.verificationNote: The relative sketch lemmas fail on zero-output examples. A separate constant-value calculation confirms failure of the supplied normalized construction. Alternative existential projections remain unrefuted.
checks.claimContext: Appendix A uses the following relative inner-product estimate for a row $u$ of the attention matrix and a value column $w^\top$, with Gaussian $R\in\mathbb R^{k\times n}$. It is the step used to justify $\widetilde P=PR^\top R$. Appendix B additionally asserts that a small scaling makes exponentiation and random projection interchangeable in its low-rank attention construction.

checks.whyItMatters: The Gaussian construction in Theorem 1 and the exponential-sketch argument in Theorem 2 do not supply their advertised probability bounds. These proofs cannot establish the stated low-rank attention guarantees as written.

checks.location: Theorems 7–8: adaptive privacy amplification by swapping and shuffling; Statements and complete proofs pp11–14
checks.claim: Theorems 7–8: adaptive privacy amplification by swapping and shuffling; Statements and complete proofs pp11–14
checks.explanation: No issue was found in the checked claims. The selected adaptive shuffling bound reconstructs after making the relevant prefix explicit.
checks.demonstration: For the swap construction, condition on the previous transcript and the swap index. At step i≥2, the current distribution is a mixture of a data-independent baseline at x_i and the exceptional x_1 randomizer, with posterior weight p. Comparing two swap indices changes at most two inputs within the observed prefix 1..i−1, so the prefix likelihood ratio is≤exp(2epsilon0); Bayes gives p≤exp(2epsilon0)/n. Mixture amplification relative to the common baseline, followed by triangle inequality between neighbouring datasets, gives per-step epsilon1=2exp(2epsilon0)(exp(epsilon0)−1)/n. Advanced composition yields the displayed bound. The final shuffle reduction is exact: fixing the sensitive entry first, uniformly permuting the other n−1 entries, and independently swapping with one of n positions produces each permutation with probability1/n!. The text says the full swapped arrays differ in at most two positions; in general three positions can differ, but only two belong to the prefix used in the likelihood calculation, which suffices for the proof.
checks.scope: Relies on the cited standard advanced composition theorem; that external theorem is not newly proved here. Does not imply the same guarantee for adaptive randomizers applied before shuffling their responses.
checks.claimContext: The swapping and shuffling constructions amplify the privacy guarantee of the stated adaptive local randomizers.

review-neurips-2026-139547.title: fev-bench: A Realistic Benchmark for Time Series Forecasting

checks.claim: Equation 4 aggregation yields rankings invariant to baseline choice.
checks.explanation: For positive errors without clipping, the baseline contributes the same term to every model's mean log error, so it cancels in pairwise comparisons. Clipping acts on the ratios after division by the baseline. Changing the baseline can therefore change which terms are clipped and reverse the model ranking.
checks.demonstration:
Consider the same two tasks and four fixed error vectors throughout:

$$E_A=(10^{-4},10^{-2}),\quad E_B=(10^{-2},10^{-4}),\quad
E_C=(10^{-4},1),\quad E_D=(1,10^{-4}).$$

Choose either $C$ or $D$ as the baseline, and compare models $A$ and $B$. Relative to $C$, clipping the two taskwise ratios gives

$$\widetilde E_A^{(C)}=(1,10^{-2}),\qquad
\widetilde E_B^{(C)}=(100,10^{-2}).$$

Their skill scores are $S_A^{(C)}=1-\sqrt{10^{-2}}=0.9$ and $S_B^{(C)}=1-\sqrt1=0$. Relative to $D$, the clipped ratios become

$$\widetilde E_A^{(D)}=(10^{-2},100),\qquad
\widetilde E_B^{(D)}=(10^{-2},1),$$

giving $S_A^{(D)}=0$ and $S_B^{(D)}=0.9$. Thus the ranking reverses. Every error is finite and strictly positive, and the tasks, model errors and task weights are unchanged. Repeating each task fifty times preserves the scores on a hundred-task collection.

The released leaderboard divides by the baseline before clipping, then calls its geometric-mean score function. That native score function reproduces the four values when supplied the clipped ratios.
checks.repair:
Restrict the invariance claim to positive errors for which clipping is inactive for every compared model under each baseline, with the tasks and weights held fixed. Let $G_j^{(\beta)}=1-S_j^{(\beta)}$ be the geometric mean relative to baseline $\beta$. With equal task weights,

$$\log G_A^{(\beta)}-\log G_B^{(\beta)}
=\frac1R\sum_{r=1}^R\log\frac{E_{rA}}{E_{rB}}.$$

The right-hand side is independent of the baseline, and the strictly decreasing transformation $S=1-G$ gives the same score ordering for every such baseline. To claim invariance for all finite positive error matrices, remove ratio clipping. If clipping is retained, describe the resulting ranking as relative to the chosen baseline.
checks.scope: The error is the unconditional baseline-invariance claim for the clipped skill score in Equation (4). The construction proves a possible ranking reversal when clipping is active; the unclipped geometric-mean argument requires positive errors and fixed tasks and weights.
checks.title: Clipping makes the skill-score ranking depend on the baseline
checks.whyItMatters: Baseline choice can affect which model ranks first under the clipped skill score. The invariance of an unclipped geometric mean cannot justify treating that choice as irrelevant.
checks.claimContext: For $R$ tasks, let $E_{rj}$ be model $j$'s error on task $r$, and let $E_{r\beta}$ be the error of a chosen baseline $\beta$. Section 4.1 defines the skill score $S_j$ by clipping each ratio $E_{rj}/E_{r\beta}$ to $[10^{-2},100]$, taking their geometric mean, and subtracting it from one. The following paragraph claims that the resulting model ranking is invariant to the baseline choice.

checks.claim: The printed revision solves signed multi-digit integer addition on all six given tests.
checks.explanation: The released interpreter and numeric comparator accept only “0 0” among the six inputs. On “5 7”, the revised program emits code point $144$ ($\mathtt{0x90}$), which is rejected for the expected output “12”. Both the literal annotated block and its instruction-only reading give the same six outputs and pass/fail results.
checks.demonstration:
The released E04 inputs are “5 7”, “-3 10”, “0 0”, “100 200”, “-50 -25” and “999 1”, with expected outputs “12”, “7”, “0”, “300”, “-75” and “1000”. A comma instruction reads one input character, including a space or minus sign; it does not parse an integer. Cell arithmetic wraps modulo $256$.

For the instruction-only revision, let $a$ and $b$ be the first two consumed character codes, and let $A$ be cell 0 after the first loop. Working modulo $256$, that loop gives $A\equiv a-48b$ and zeros cell 1. The second loop puts $-48A$ in cell 1 and zeros cell 0. The next loop transfers that value back. The final loop adds eight and multiplies by six, so the output code point $y$ is

$$y\equiv6(-48A+8)\equiv48-32a\pmod{256}.$$

The coefficient of $b$ vanishes modulo $256$. For “5 7”, $a=53$ and $y=144$. The six native outputs have code points $(144,144,48,16,144,16)$; only $48$, the character “0” on the third test, passes.

The literal annotation “a, b” adds an active comma instruction. Executing the entire printed block and, separately, only the instruction lines produces the same output list. An independent bounded byte interpreter agrees with the native interpreter for both readings on all six tests.

The native Brainfuck matcher accepts a decimal integer with an optional minus sign and surrounding whitespace, then compares integer values. It accepts, for example, “ 012” followed by a newline for expected “12”; it rejects the single code point $144$. Thus the counterexample also holds under numeric equivalence. The printed initial-program feedback needs correction too: the native outputs for the first three inputs are “U”, a grave accent, and “P”, rather than the bytes or runtime error shown in J.3.
checks.repair:
Correct both feedback excerpts in Appendix J.3 and describe the revision as a failed repair: it passes only “0 0” among the six E04 tests. Show all six input–output pairs for each displayed iteration, and replace the success, early-exit and closing byte-comparison claims with the actual interpreter outputs and numeric grading rule.

A successful worked example would need a program that parses both signed decimal integers and prints their decimal sum. Supply its exact executed source, interpreter version and six test outputs so the program, feedback and claimed outcome agree.

review-neurips-2026-148237.title: STRIDE: Learnable Stepwise Language Feedback for LLM Reasoning

checks.location: Section 5.2, Sensitivity and Verifier Quality Assessment; equation (2)
checks.claim: Only successes update GRPO and consequently redirection cannot harm performance.
checks.explanation: A failed continuation has a negative, nonzero advantage whenever its group contains a success. Correct outcome rewards therefore do not select only successes for gradient updates. They also do not prevent a shared-parameter update that improves redirected continuations from reducing success on ordinary prompts.
checks.demonstration:
Take the paper’s group size $K=5$ with outcome rewards $(1,0,0,0,0)$. The mean is $1/5$. Under population standard deviation $2/5$, Equation (2) gives a failed sample advantage $(-1/5)/(2/5+\epsilon)<0$. The publicly dispatched `compute_grpo_advantage` uses sample standard deviation $1/\sqrt5$ instead, giving

$$\widehat A_{\mathrm{success}}=\frac{4/5}{1/\sqrt5+10^{-6}}\approx1.788850,
\qquad\widehat A_{\mathrm{failure}}=\frac{-1/5}{1/\sqrt5+10^{-6}}\approx-0.447213.$$

Both conventions contradict success-only updates. In the released refinement path, the batch is scored, normalized and passed to the actor update without filtering out failed continuations. The function named `compute_grpo_outcome_advantage` is not the function dispatched by this path. Equal-reward groups have zero task advantages under this normalization.

A separate shared-parameter example refutes the performance guarantee. Let an ordinary prompt have probability $\sigma(\theta)$ of its correct action and a redirected prompt have probability $\sigma(-\theta)$ of its correct action, where $\sigma(t)=1/(1+e^{-t})$. Both outcomes are scored exactly. Training contains only the redirected context; evaluation contains only the ordinary prompt. Each context offers two one-token actions, with reward one for the correct action and zero for the other. At $\theta=0$, use the mixed group above for the redirected prompt. The correct action has log-probability derivative $-1/2$ and an incorrect action has derivative $1/2$. The gradient of the mean GRPO surrogate is therefore

$$g=\frac15\left(-\frac12\widehat A_{\mathrm{success}}+4\cdot\frac12\widehat A_{\mathrm{failure}}\right)\approx-0.357770.$$

At the old policy all importance ratios equal one, so clipping is locally inactive. If the reference policy is also the initial policy, the KL term has zero gradient there. An entropy bonus also has zero derivative at this symmetric binary policy. Neither regularizer cancels the displayed first-step gradient. A gradient-ascent step of size $0.1$ yields $\theta'\approx-0.035777$. Ordinary-prompt success decreases from $0.5$ to $0.491057$, while redirected-prompt success increases to $0.508943$. The two contexts are distinct inputs to the same parameterized policy, exactly the possibility a universal harmlessness claim must control. The sign persists for arbitrarily small positive step sizes. At the configured learning rate $10^{-6}$, the first one-dimensional AdamW step from zero also moves $\theta$ negative (approximately $-10^{-6}$), lowering ordinary-prompt success to $0.49999975$; weight decay is zero at the initial parameter.

The reward vector is a possible sampled group: five independent continuations at the initial policy have exactly one success with probability $5/32$. More generally, with $h\in\{1,2,3,4\}$ successes, put $d_h=\sqrt{h(5-h)/20}+10^{-6}$. The sample-standard-deviation advantages give

$$g_h=-\frac{h(5-h)}{25d_h}<0.$$

Every mixed group therefore lowers ordinary-prompt success after a sufficiently small positive step, while the two equal-reward groups have zero task gradient. Mixed groups have probability $1-2(1/2)^5=15/16$. Averaging the explicit size-$0.1$ steps over all six success counts gives ordinary-prompt success approximately $0.490360$, below $1/2$. Redirected-context success increases. The failure concerns a guarantee across shared-parameter contexts, not a claim that exact rewards make the redirected objective worse. The same sign holds for arbitrarily small steps, including the configured learning rate.
checks.repair:
State Equation (2)'s consequence directly: equal-reward groups have zero task advantages; in a mixed binary-reward group, successes have positive advantages and failures have negative advantages. Keep the all-failure special case in Section 4.3. Remove the universal harmlessness guarantee and its success-only explanation wherever used in the abstract, Sections 4.3 and 5.2, Appendix D.1 and the repository summary. KL, entropy and optimizer state are separate from task advantages and can change parameters even when those advantages vanish.

A guarantee about ordinary-prompt performance requires an explicit evaluation distribution, assumptions controlling shared-parameter interference, and a proved update rule for that objective. Filtering failures is insufficient: increasing the likelihood of the successful redirected action alone also decreases ordinary-prompt success in the example.

These changes leave Equation (2) and the training algorithm intact and correct the properties attributed to them. They withdraw the universal guarantee rather than restore it.
checks.scope: The finding concerns STRIDE’s success-only update explanation and its universal harmless-improvement claim. Negative task advantages for failures in mixed groups are standard GRPO behavior, not a new defect in GRPO. All-failure groups still have zero task advantages. The shared-parameter example lowers ordinary-prompt success while improving the redirected context. Pith already criticized the same harmlessness guarantee in May 2026 with a different argument.
checks.whyItMatters: The paper advertises robustness to imperfect verifiers as a design guarantee. Group normalization and shared parameters do not provide that guarantee.
checks.title: Outcome-only GRPO does not imply success-only or harmless updates
checks.claimContext: In Phase III, STRIDE samples redirected continuations and trains the same generator parameters used for ordinary prompts. Equation (2) defines a group-normalized task advantage $\widehat A_k$ from binary outcome correctness $c_k^*\in\{0,1\}$, group size $K$ and stabilizer $\epsilon>0$. Section 5.2 infers that only successful redirections contribute gradients and that improvement is non-negative by design. Section 4.3’s narrower observation is valid: a group in which every task reward is zero has zero task advantages.
checks.checkedLocation: Equation (2) and Section 4.3, p.6; Section 5.2 Sensitivity and Verifier Quality Assessment, p.9; Appendix D.1; pinned refinement and GRPO callers.

checks.claim: Linear readout of pooled first/second monomials represents every invariant quadratic.
checks.explanation: A linear readout can combine the pooled first and second moments, but it cannot multiply pooled first moments. Those products are needed for quadratic interactions between different units. Permutation invariance does not remove these interactions.
checks.demonstration: Take two scalar units with $K=[0,1]$ and target $G(x_1,x_2)=(x_1+x_2)^2$. The domain is compact, and $G$ is continuous, quadratic, and unchanged by exchanging the units. The pooled features are $m=(x_1+x_2)/2$ and $q=(x_1^2+x_2^2)/2$. Even allowing an intercept, a linear readout has the form $H=a+bm+cq$. At the four inputs $(0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)$, every such $H$ satisfies $$H(1,1)-H(1,0)-H(0,1)+H(0,0)=0.$$ The same expression for $G$ equals $4-1-1+0=2$. Thus no affine readout of these pooled features represents this admissible invariant quadratic.
checks.repair: Allow a polynomial readout of degree at most two. This preserves the pooled feature map and exactly represents every invariant quadratic for fixed $M$. To see this, let $m=M^{-1}\sum_i x_i$ and $Q=M^{-1}\sum_i x_ix_i^\top$. Averaging any quadratic representation over unit permutations preserves its values and gives each scalar invariant quadratic the form $$G=c+b^\top\sum_i x_i+\sum_i x_i^\top A x_i+\sum_{i\ne j}x_i^\top Bx_j,$$ with symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$. Hence $$G=c+M b^\top m+M\operatorname{tr}((A-B)Q)+M^2m^\top Bm.$$ The last term is quadratic in the pooled first moment; the other terms are affine in the pooled features. Vector-valued targets follow coordinatewise. For the counterexample, $\rho(m,q)=4m^2$. If a linear readout is required, restrict the claim to invariant quadratics without cross-unit interaction terms.
checks.scope: The failure concerns the linear-readout quadratic remark in Appendix A.2. It does not contradict the fixed-$M$ expressivity proposition with a continuous readout. A quadratic readout restores the full class of invariant quadratic targets without adding per-unit features.
checks.title: Invariant quadratics can require a quadratic readout

checks.claim: Uniform steering distribution forces JS divergence to zero and removes the alignment gradient.
checks.explanation: For a fixed mixture weight $0<\alpha<1$, Jensen–Shannon divergence vanishes when the two distributions agree, not when just the steering distribution is uniform. A nonuniform target leaves a positive disagreement term and can give a nonzero gradient at uniform steering.
checks.demonstration:
Take $\alpha=1/2$, $p_S=(1/2,1/2)$, and $p_B=(0.9,0.1)$. Their mixture is $(0.7,0.3)$, so

$$\operatorname{JS}_{1/2}(p_S,p_B)\approx0.10175>0.$$

Let the steering probabilities be $(\sigma(\delta),1-\sigma(\delta))$, where $\sigma$ is the logistic function. At $\delta=0$, steering is uniform and its entropy derivative is zero. With the target detached, the divergence derivative is instead

$$\left.\frac{d}{d\delta}\operatorname{JS}_{1/2}\right|_{\delta=0}=\frac18\log\!\left(\frac{0.3}{0.7}\right)\ne0.$$

Thus the disagreement contribution need not disappear even at exact uniformity.
checks.repair: Use agreement, $p_S=p_B$, as the condition for a zero Jensen–Shannon term at an interior mixture weight. If the intended failure is weak input adaptation, formulate it in terms of the steering model’s probability Jacobian with respect to the input or prompt. A small Jacobian can make the input gradient small even when disagreement remains positive; uniform output probabilities alone do not imply that condition. Keep this distinction when explaining the empirical failure regime.
checks.scope: This corrects the proposed mechanism in one failure-mode explanation. The paper’s entropy–Jensen–Shannon identity remains valid.
checks.claimContext: Appendix E attributes one BETA failure regime to nearly uniform steering predictions. It says the Jensen–Shannon term then approaches zero and the effective objective reduces to steering entropy. The method mixes steering probabilities $p_S$ with detached target probabilities $p_B$.
checks.title: Uniform steering predictions do not eliminate the disagreement term
checks.whyItMatters: Uniform predictions, agreement between models, and an uninformative adaptation gradient are different properties. The failure analysis currently treats them as equivalent.

checks.claim: The logarithmic coupon-collection bound suffices for the filtered population graph.
checks.explanation: The proof bounds the chance of an unobserved transition, but the filtered algorithm can also remove an observed singleton. Seeing every population transition once therefore does not guarantee recovery of the final extracted graph.
checks.demonstration:
Let traces be $ab$ with probability $0.99$ and $ac$ with probability $0.01$. The population graph has three transitions: the initial $a$, then its two possible successors. Set $p_{\min}=0.01$ and $\delta=0.05$. The claimed sufficient sample size is $N=410$.

Let $K$ count the rare $ac$ traces. If $K=0$, the rare edge is absent. If $K=1$, it is removed by the singleton filter because the common continuation is also present. Thus failure probability is at least

$$\Pr(K\le1)=0.99^{410}+410(0.01)0.99^{409}\approx0.083>0.05.$$

The traces are independent and meet the stated minimum appearance probability.
checks.repair:
Apply the original coupon bound to the unfiltered Steps 1–2, or require enough traces that every transition appears in at least two independent traces. A sufficient condition for the filtered algorithm is

$$r\left[(1-p_{\min})^N+Np_{\min}(1-p_{\min})^{N-1}\right]\le\delta.$$

For each transition, its trace-appearance count is binomial with probability at least $p_{\min}$. The bracket bounds its chance of appearing at most once; a union bound over $r$ transitions proves recovery because none can be singleton-filtered. This changes the finite-sample condition while preserving the target population graph.
checks.scope: The finite-sample guarantee does not apply to the filtered algorithm as written. The stronger count bound repairs it under the same independent-trace model. Eventual convergence and the coupon bound for the unfiltered directly-follows graph are not contradicted.
checks.claimContext: Proposition 5 claims exact recovery of the population directly-follows automaton $\mathcal M^*$ from independent traces. Let $r$ be its transition count, $p_{\min}$ a lower bound on each transition’s probability of appearing in one trace, and $\delta$ the allowed failure probability. The extraction algorithm removes a transition observed exactly once when its source has another continuation. All states accept, so this issue concerns the transition graph rather than termination labels.
checks.title: Singleton filtering requires more than observing each transition once
checks.whyItMatters: A recovery theorem must account for transitions that preprocessing deliberately deletes, as well as transitions the sample never contains.

checks.claim: IID traces alone imply a multinomial concentration bound in total state visits n_q.
checks.explanation: Independence between traces does not prevent all transitions within one trace from sharing a hidden random choice. Counting those dependent visits as independent observations can make the stated error probability arbitrarily too small.
checks.demonstration:
Draw one trace as $(ab)^{1000}$ or $(ac)^{1000}$, each with probability $1/2$. This satisfies the i.i.d.-trace premise. At the state recording $a$, there are $n_q=1000$ visits, but all choose the same next symbol. In alphabet order $(a,b,c)$, the population transition law is

$$P^*=(0,1/2,1/2).$$

With additive smoothing $\alpha=1$, the estimate is $(1,1001,1)/1003$, or its swap of $b,c$. In either case,

$$\|\widehat P-P^*\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=\frac{1001}{2006}>0.499.$$

For $\epsilon=0.2$, the event in the proposition has probability one: its threshold is $0.2+3/1003<0.203$. The claimed upper bound is $6e^{-20}<1.3\times10^{-8}$. The discrepancy comes from dependence, rather than smoothing.
checks.repair:
State the sampling unit explicitly. For a fixed number $n$ of independent categorical visits over $m$ symbols, coordinatewise Hoeffding bounds give the valid, conservative replacement

$$\Pr\!\left(\|\widehat P-P^*\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\ge\epsilon+\frac{m\alpha}{n+m\alpha}\right)\le2m\exp\!\left(-\frac{8n\epsilon^2}{m^2}\right).$$

For independent traces with dependent visits, prove a trace-level or mixing bound instead. Its effective sample size must account for within-trace dependence. A visit-count rate cannot be imported from a multinomial model without that additional premise.
checks.scope: The exponential rate in Proposition 6 is false under independence of traces alone. The corrected bound applies under independent state visits. It does not establish the same rate for the paper’s general trace model, or contradict eventual consistency when the number of independent traces grows under suitable moment conditions.
checks.claimContext: Proposition 6 assumes an i.i.d. distribution of complete traces and bounds transition-estimation error using the number $n_q$ of visits to state $q$. It treats the pooled transition counts as multinomial observations. The preceding automaton construction records the last activity and allows repeated visits within a trace.
checks.title: Independent traces do not give independent state visits
checks.whyItMatters: A long run can repeat one random decision many times. Those repetitions should not be credited as many independent training examples.

checks.claim: Normalized per-trace cross-entropy difference is an optimal likelihood-ratio statistic without equal-length restriction.
checks.explanation: The likelihood ratio multiplies evidence over the entire trace. Dividing its logarithm by a variable trace length can merge traces that have different likelihood ratios. More training data does not recover the information removed by that normalization.
checks.demonstration:
Let the next symbol be independent of the current state, with $P^+(a)=1/2$ and $P^-(a)=3/4$. Let trace length be independently $1$ or $2$, with the same distribution in both classes. This can be represented on the paper’s last-activity states by assigning the same transition row to each state.

The common length probabilities cancel in the likelihood ratio. Traces $a$ and $aa$ therefore have ratios

$$\frac{P^-(a)}{P^+(a)}=\frac32,\qquad\frac{P^-(aa)}{P^+(aa)}=\frac94.$$

A likelihood-ratio test at threshold $2$ separates these two cases. Their average cross-entropy differences are both $-\log_2(3/2)$, so a threshold on that average cannot implement the test. This example uses the exact class models.
checks.repair:
Use the total log-likelihood ratio

$$L(\tau)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log\frac{P^-(a_t\mid q_t)}{P^+(a_t\mid q_t)},$$

adding initial-state and length-likelihood terms when these differ between classes. At one fixed length with common initial and length laws, the average cross-entropy difference is a monotone rescaling of $L$ and can be used instead. For estimated probabilities, require positive lower bounds and quantify the resulting error in the total log ratio; classification accuracy also depends on the probability mass near the decision threshold.
checks.scope: The variable-length optimality claim fails even with exact probabilities. A fixed-length likelihood-ratio formulation is valid under the stated Markov class model and common initial law. For a fixed observed trace, increasing training data estimates that trace’s realized cross-entropy; estimating an expectation over new traces is a separate sampling question.
checks.title: Length normalization can discard likelihood-ratio information
checks.claimContext: Corollary 7 considers success and failure transition models $P^+$ and $P^-$ on one FSM state space. It calls the difference of their per-step cross-entropies a Neyman–Pearson-optimal trace statistic. The statement does not require equal trace lengths.
checks.whyItMatters: Two matching observations generally provide more classification evidence than one. A per-step average can hide that difference.

checks.claim: A single fixed likelihood-ratio threshold enjoys sublinear regret versus the best state-dependent threshold in hindsight for any B-Lipschitz loss.
checks.explanation: Bounded likelihood increments do not make a fixed threshold competitive with other thresholds under every loss. The monitor does not implement the policy-learning procedure needed for an expert or bandit regret bound. Moreover, the displayed training-error term is linear in $T$ when $n_q$ is fixed.
checks.demonstration:
Take a singleton alphabet $\{a\}$ and the two states consisting of the initial state and the last-$a$ state. Both success and failure classes emit only $a$. The failure label $Y$ is constant along a trace, with $\Pr(Y=1)=0.9$. All estimated transition probabilities are exactly one, including with additive smoothing, so $L_t=0$.

Threshold $\eta=1$ always predicts success. The admissible state-independent comparator $\eta_q=-1$ declares failure immediately; the proposition imposes no sign restriction on its thresholds. For $\ell_t(y)=|y-Y|$, a $1$-Lipschitz loss, their expected cumulative losses are $0.9T$ and $0.1T$. Regret against the best hindsight comparator is therefore at least

$$0.8T.$$

At $T=100$, $B=1$ and at least $n_q=10{,}000$ training observations per state, the proposed right-hand side is $\sqrt{200\log2}+1<13$, whereas regret is at least $80$.
checks.repair:
Remove the regret claim for an arbitrary fixed threshold. A valid alternative requires a different learning rule: specify a finite family of $K$ candidate prediction policies, observe per-step labels and losses in $[0,1]$, and use exponential weights to aggregate those policies. That forecaster satisfies

$$\mathbb E R_T\le\frac{\log K}{\eta_{\mathrm{learn}}}+\frac{\eta_{\mathrm{learn}}T}{8},$$

which becomes $\sqrt{T\log K/2}$ at the optimal learning rate. The comparator count is $K$, not the number of FSM states. This repair needs feedback and an aggregation algorithm; it does not give the original stopping monitor a regret bound.
checks.scope: Proposition 8’s fixed-threshold regret guarantee fails under its stated mixture and loss assumptions. The proposed expert-learning theorem is a different guarantee with additional feedback requirements. Neither a regret rate nor bounded likelihood increments alone establishes the empirical monitor’s time to detect a failure.
checks.claimContext: Proposition 8 monitors the cumulative estimated log-likelihood ratio $L_t$ and declares failure when it first exceeds a fixed threshold $\eta$. With per-step log ratios bounded by $B$, equation 9 claims regret against the best state-dependent threshold policy in hindsight for any $B$-Lipschitz loss.
checks.title: A fixed alarm threshold has no general hindsight-regret guarantee
checks.whyItMatters: A detector’s likelihood score and a policy-learning algorithm answer different questions. A performance bound must describe the decision rule that is actually used.

checks.claim: Encoding the FSM transition table instead of corpus traces establishes a superior MDL/compression ratio.
checks.explanation: A transition table summarizes which continuations exist, and possibly their counts. It does not determine the order of the observed traces. Omitting the residual data-given-model code compares objects carrying different information, so the table size alone cannot establish a lossless or MDL advantage for the corpus.
checks.demonstration: There are 17,640 distinct binary strings of length 20 with the same initial symbol $a$ and the same transition counts $aa=5$, $ab=5$, $ba=5$, $bb=4$. To see the count directly, each such string consists of six positive-length $a$ runs and five positive-length $b$ runs, starting and ending with $a$. There are 11 occurrences of $a$ and 9 of $b$, giving $\binom{10}{5}\binom{8}{4}=252\cdot70=17{,}640$ choices of run lengths. All four transitions occur repeatedly, so singleton filtering does not distinguish them. Even the counted FSM is identical for these strings. Any fixed-length or binary prefix code distinguishing all of them needs at least $\lceil\log_2 17{,}640\rceil=15$ bits in the worst case; under a uniform distribution their conditional entropy is $\log_2 17{,}640\approx14.1066$ bits.

A normalized probabilistic trace model can provide the residual through a prefix or arithmetic code, with its coding overhead included. Compare complete codes for the same data. checks.demonstration:
Use a two-outcome logistic policy with probabilities $p$ and $1-p$, and a sampled group containing one of each outcome. Take rewards $R_1=1$, $R_2=1/2$, baseline $c=0$, and sharpness $\kappa=1$. These rewards are bounded. The supplementary cooling rule gives

$$w_1=\frac{p}{1+p},\qquad w_2=\frac{1-p}{2-p}.$$

As $p\downarrow0$, the rare outcome's negative log likelihood tends to infinity and $w_1\to0$. Nevertheless,

$$A_1=\frac{w_1R_1-w_2R_2}{2}\longrightarrow-\frac18.$$

Its log-score derivative with respect to its logit is $1-p\to1$. Including the group factor, its gradient contribution tends to $-1/16$, rather than zero. The corresponding uncooled contribution tends to $1/8$, so the ratio of gradient norms tends to $1/2$, rather than an exponentially vanishing value. The specified group has positive sampling probability for every $p>0$.

$$\|w_i(R_i-b_i)\nabla\log\pi_i\|\le MC\,e^{\kappa c}e^{-\kappa\ell_i}.$$

review-neurips-2026-149601.title: Euclidean Embedding of Data Using Local Distances

checks.location: Appendix D (proof of Theorem 1), paragraph before Eq. (46)
checks.claim: Because J is convex in d(phi) and 'convex with respect to Q', monotone decrease of J along the alternating scheme (8) implies convergence to the global minimum (Theorem 1).
checks.explanation: Exact minimization of each block decreases the objective, but the orthogonality constraint makes the joint problem nonconvex. Here the issue is stronger than a missing convergence argument: the prescribed initialization reaches an explicit fixed point with positive error although zero error is feasible.
checks.demonstration:
Let $\Omega=\{(r,\theta):1<r<2\}$ be the connected flat annulus, and write $R(\theta)$ for planar rotation through angle $\theta$. Choose the smooth row of one-forms
$$\alpha=(dx,dy)R(-\theta).$$
This coframe is pointwise orthonormal and hence metric-trivializing. The optimization allows $Q$ to be a pointwise orthogonal field, as in Eqs. (7b) and Appendix C. Start at the prescribed initialization $Q_0=I$.

The first Neumann minimization has, up to additive constants, the solution
$$\varphi(r,\theta)=f(r)(\cos2\theta,\sin2\theta),\qquad f(r)=\frac r3+\frac{7r^2}{45}-\frac8{45r^2}.$$
Direct differentiation gives
$$r^2f''+rf'-4f=-r,\qquad f'(1)=f'(2)=1.$$
These identities verify the required divergence equation and normal boundary traces on both boundary components. The boundary condition is the outward-normal contraction defined in Appendix A. Additive constants do not affect the subsequent alignment step.

Let $A=R(\theta)$ be the row-coefficient matrix of the coframe. The matrix used for the pointwise SVD update is
$$D\varphi A^\top=R(2\theta)\operatorname{diag}\left(f'(r),\frac{2f(r)}r\right)R(-2\theta).$$
It is positive definite throughout the annulus. Indeed,
$$f'(r)=\frac13+\frac{14r}{45}+\frac{16}{45r^3}>0,$$
and $f(1)=14/45>0$, so $f(r)>0$ for $1<r<2$. Its polar factor is consequently the identity, and Eq. (8b) returns $Q_1=I$. Every later block update repeats the same pair. The objective at this fixed point is
$$J=2\pi\int_1^2\left[(f'(r)-1)^2+\left(\frac{2f(r)}r-1\right)^2\right]r\,dr=0.302523737\ldots>0.$$

In contrast, $\varphi(x,y)=(x,y)$ with $Q=R(\theta)$ aligns the coframe exactly and gives $J=0$. Thus the mandated initialization reaches a fixed point above the global minimum. The trial map in the fixed point covers the angle twice, but the stated variational class imposes no injectivity condition; its unconstrained Neumann block solver would not enforce one either. Blockwise minimization still ensures nonincreasing nonnegative objective values. It does not imply the claimed global optimum, uniqueness up to rigid motions, or convergence of all iterates.
checks.repair: Retain the blockwise objective-descent statement: each exact block minimization cannot increase the nonnegative objective, so its values converge. This does not imply that the iterates converge or that their limit is a global minimum. A global-optimality theorem needs additional assumptions or a different optimization argument excluding the explicit nonglobal fixed point. No such replacement theorem is established.
checks.scope: The contradiction concerns the global-minimizer conclusion of Theorem 1 and Appendix D. The construction uses the stated Neumann and pointwise alignment equations without changing them.
checks.title: The alternating embedding update can stop above the global minimum
checks.claimContext: The method alternates a Neumann solve for the embedding coordinates with a pointwise orthogonal alignment. Theorem 1 claims that the prescribed initialization $Q_0=I$ converges to global minimizers.
checks.whyItMatters: The central global-convergence guarantee fails on a smooth, admissible manifold and from the required initialization.
checks.checkedLocation: Theorem 1, Eqs. (7)–(8), Appendices A, C and D

checks.location: Section3.2.1 before Theorem6 and its proof; Definition7
checks.claim: Absence of weakly dominated actions as defined in Definition7 ensures all labeled actions survive positive-orthant polarization; Theorem6 characterizes the full BR-indistinguishability set using extreme points alone.
checks.explanation: An action can be dominated by a mixture without being dominated by another pure action. Such an action can be a vertex of the original utility polytope $\mathcal P_i$ but cease to be a vertex after adding the nonpositive orthant $C_i^\circ$. Extreme points of the polarized polyhedron then lose an action label required by the theorem's set equality.
checks.demonstration:
Consider an agent with three actions and two opponent actions, with utility vectors $v_1=(0,1)$, $v_2=(1/4,1/4)$ and $v_3=(1,0)$. Each pair has a strict payoff tradeoff, so Definition 7 excludes none of the actions. The three vectors are noncollinear and are all vertices of their convex hull. Yet the equal mixture of actions 1 and 3 has vector $(1/2,1/2)$, exceeding $v_2$ by $1/4$ in each coordinate. Therefore, at every belief $(t,1-t)$ with $0\leq t\leq1$, the middle action has payoff $1/4$, while the mixture has payoff $1/2$. At least one of the two endpoint actions strictly beats the middle action.

Let $P=\operatorname{conv}\{v_1,v_2,v_3\}$ and $Q=P+\mathbb R_-^2$. The points $(1/2,0)$ and $(0,1/2)$ belong to $Q$, and their midpoint is $v_2$. Thus $v_2$ is not extreme in $Q$; indeed $Q=\operatorname{conv}\{v_1,v_3\}+\mathbb R_-^2$ has only two vertices. Every polyhedron with this normal fan also has two vertices, so the theorem’s vertex labeling cannot recover the original three-action game, even though that game is indistinguishable from itself. To embed the example in a full two-player game, give the second player utility vectors $(1,0,0)$ and $(0,1,1)$; neither is pure-action dominated. The strict mixture advantage and pairwise payoff tradeoffs persist under small perturbations, so genericity cannot remove the defect.
checks.repair:
For the vertex-based characterization, require every labeled action to be the unique best response to some strictly positive belief. Match the resulting vertices by their labeled best-response cones.

This assumption prevents the lost-action defect. If $y>0$ uniquely exposes utility vector $v$, adding a nonzero vector from $\mathbb R_-^d$ strictly reduces its inner product with $y$. Thus $v$ stays exposed in the polarized polyhedron. Conversely, each vertex of a polytope plus a pointed cone comes from a vertex of that polytope. These two facts restore the action-to-vertex correspondence for the restricted class.

To retain Definition 7's broader class, store the utility vectors of never-best-response actions separately and require equality of the best-response region for every action label. Extreme points alone cannot retain those labels.
checks.scope: The false implication is the action-to-vertex step in Theorem 6 under Definition 7's pure-action nondominance condition. Unique exposure by a strictly positive belief restores that step for a narrower class, with labels matched through best-response cones. Retaining the original class requires separate information for nonvertex action labels. The separate quantal-response theorem and regret bounds are not contradicted by this example.
checks.title: Pure-action nondominance does not preserve every action under polarization
checks.claimContext: Definition 7 excludes domination by another pure action. Theorem 6 represents the full labeled best-response indistinguishability set using extreme points of polyhedra normally equivalent to $\widetilde{\mathcal P}_i=\mathcal P_i+C_i^\circ$, where $C_i=\mathbb R_+^{d_i}$. Here $\sigma$ assigns action labels to vertices and $\mathcal N$ denotes the normal fan. The proof assumes every action remains a vertex after adding the nonpositive orthant.
checks.whyItMatters: Theorem 6 claims to describe all games with the same labeled best responses. In the example, polarization reduces three action vertices to two, so the proposed representation cannot even encode the original three-action game, which must belong to its own indistinguishability set.

review-neurips-2026-156795.title: The Confusion is Real: GRAPHIC – A Network Science Approach to Confusion Matrices in Deep Learning

checks.location: Section 4.2 lambda=0 paragraph (cached newline lines 704–707); Appendix A.3 line 1749
checks.claim: Training a linear probe only on model-predicted labels prevents it from exceeding the model true-label accuracy.
checks.explanation: Population fitting can remove teacher errors that are nonlinear in the frozen features.
checks.demonstration: Let $x=\pm1$ and $u\in\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$ be independent uniform variables, with true label $\mathbf1_{x=1}$. The teacher flips it when $|u|=2$, so has 60% accuracy. On features $(x,u)$, the population pseudo-label cross-entropy minimizer has logit $\log(1.5)x$: balanced symmetry makes its gradient zero and convexity makes it global. Its classifications recover every true label without true-label training.
checks.repair: Describe teacher replication as a possible outcome rather than a universal accuracy ceiling.
checks.scope: This is a counterexample to the ceiling, not a claim that every pseudo-label probe improves its teacher.

review-neurips-2026-156795.issueTitle: A pseudo-label probe can exceed its teacher's true-label accuracy
review-neurips-2026-156795.plainExplanation: A linear probe trained only on pseudo-labels can denoise nonlinear teacher errors in frozen features and exceed the teacher's true-label accuracy. The claimed universal ceiling therefore does not follow from label provenance.
